extracted.intended_audience: Associated Press members, newspaper publishers, journalists, and interested general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Report of Associated Press board and membership decisions on news-exchange contracts, service to governments, membership categories, antitrust exposure, and principles of objective reporting. Focuses on rules and practices governing how AP permits use and transmission of its news and who may be an AP member.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on providing propaganda for governments
rubrics_metrics.description: The service which the State Department plans to put out will not be propaganda but a fair presentation of the Associated Press report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board statement: AP held that any broadcast designed to promote 'our way of life' would of necessity be from an American viewpoint and 'certainly not objective news presentation.' Consequently the AP decided to end (or renegotiate) service to the State Department for short-wave purposes to avoid being used as government propaganda; original wartime arrangement was extended but reconsidered. Anti-pattern: furnishing news that is intended primarily as government propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of reciprocal exchange with foreign press agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: AP principle of exchange of news with the press or agencies of the press of all countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts and exchanges should generally follow the principle of news exchange among agencies worldwide, but may include country-specific contractual limits (see domestic-use restrictions and the Tass example). The board framed action to keep exchanges aligned with this principle while guarding against misuse for propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual restriction on retransmission (Tass example)
rubrics_metrics.description: AP exchange of news contract with the Russian Tass agency specifically bars Tass from retransmitting AP news outside of Russia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example used to justify that some contracts can lawfully and properly restrict foreign retransmission. Shows how bilateral contracts can permit exchange while limiting downstream use; analogous restrictions being applied or renegotiated with other agencies (e.g., Canadian Press, BBC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit foreign contracts to domestic-use only
rubrics_metrics.description: Renegotiate all contracts to provide only for the domestic use within their own borders of Associated Press news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board instructed renegotiation of contracts (Canadian Press, BBC, etc.) to prevent AP news being included in foreign transmissions or international propaganda; specific outcomes: Canadian Press not permitted to include AP news in foreign transmissions when arrangement ends; BBC arrangement not to be renewed except for domestic broadcasting in England. Anti-pattern: permitting broad international retransmission that could be used for propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership classes and eligibility (associate membership)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain classes of users of news to be eligible for associate membership: (a) owners of radio stations and (b) persons, firms and corporations engaged in the publication of news and which now have or may hereafter have news exchange arrangements with the AP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership-rule change approved by vote (173 to 14) expanding eligibility to defined associate members. Guidance includes examples of organizations admitted (several local papers). This is a procedural rubric for who may qualify as AP members or associate members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve editorial objectivity and nonpartisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: The Associated Press neither has favored nor opposed any movement; the board of directors has held almost unanimously that this is no time to make a departure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board emphasized maintaining unbiased news and refusing to 'make a departure' from impartial reporting despite outside pressures. Anti-pattern: AP taking partisan positions or actively promoting causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion to select customers vs. antitrust exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal that anti-trust laws should not be construed to prohibit any press service company 'from exercising its own discretion in the selection of its customers' or from furnishing its press services on conditions not to furnish services to the customer's competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The resolution proposed amending law to protect AP's discretion; board noted legal risk and debated whether duty to serve all applicants without discrimination should be legislative rather than judicial. Includes quotes from publishers and a federal judge on legal implications. Anti-pattern: being legally forced by court rulings to provide services without discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid financial dependence on government as primary backer
rubrics_metrics.description: The board warned that accepting government payment for services could 'at once make the Government the heaviest financial backer of the Associated Press.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial consideration is a criterion in deciding whether to furnish gratis or paid services to governments. Board cited the AP's costs (e.g., three‑year cost of government anti-trust suit was $474,314.55) and warned against arrangements that would compromise independence by making government a dominant funder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal compliance and managing anti-trust litigation risk
rubrics_metrics.description: AP must consider anti-trust litigation, associated legal fees and the possibility of seeking legislative remedies rather than being bound by judicial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board referenced ongoing anti-trust suit, the cost of litigation, and the need to renegotiate contracts to reduce exposure. Guidance includes suggestion to seek Congressional amendment to clarify that press services may exercise selection discretion; anti-pattern: allowing unresolved legal exposure to dictate editorial or business policies without seeking legal or legislative remedies.
